title: S6 — Roofing and Wind-Resistant Detailing (The Hurricane Module)

concepts.title: Wind lifts roofs off — it does not push them down
concepts.mechanism: When wind blows over a roof it speeds up, and fast-moving air has LOWER pressure — the same reason a plane's wing lifts. So a hurricane does not push your roof down; it SUCKS it up, hardest at the edges and corners. If the roof is not tied down to the walls, and the walls to the foundation, in one continuous chain, the wind finds the weakest link and peels the whole thing off — usually starting at a corner.
concepts.mechanismPro: Aerodynamic uplift; suction peaks at eaves, ridges and corners (higher GCp). Design a continuous load path: roof covering → deck → rafters → hurricane straps → wall → hold-downs → foundation. The connections, not the members, are what fail — every link must carry the uplift.
concepts.hook: Hold a sheet of paper by one edge and blow across the TOP — it rises toward the fast air, it does not get pushed down. Your roof is that paper in a hurricane.

applied.prompt: To save cost, a sub proposes toe-nailing the rafters to the wall plate instead of the specified hurricane straps — in a hurricane-strength wind zone. Your call?

options.label: Hold the spec — engineered straps, continuous from roof to foundation
options.outcome: Right. Toe-nails pull straight out under uplift; straps are the link that carries it. The continuous tie-down is the difference between a roof that stays and one in the neighbour's yard.

options.label: Allow toe-nails but add more of them
options.outcome: More nails loaded the wrong way (in withdrawal) still pull out — you cannot fix a bad connection type with quantity. This is the failure mode that fills post-storm reports.

options.label: Allow it to save money — it is just the roof-to-wall joint
options.outcome: That 'just' joint is the link the entire uplift path runs through. Break it and the roof leaves, the walls follow, and the interior is destroyed. The cheapest connection on the job, and the one that loses the building.

applied.debrief: Wind is an uplift problem, and uplift is a load-path problem: an unbroken chain from roof to ground, with the CONNECTIONS as the weak links to detail hardest. Corners and edges see the most suction — tie them down like the building depends on it, because it does.

summary: Wind uplift must travel roof covering → sheathing → truss → strap → ring beam → wall steel → footing → rock, with every link CONNECTED. Hurricanes fail the weakest link, and the weakest link is almost always a connection. PLAIN: the storm tries to pull the roof off; every part must hold the next. PRO: load path, zone nailing, strap schedules, opening protection as structure.

sections.heading: The load path is the exam question
sections.body: PLAIN: In a storm, the roof is a wing — air rushing over it pulls UP. That pull has to be handed down, piece to piece, all the way to the rock: covering to sheathing, sheathing to truss, truss to strap, strap to ring beam, ring beam to wall steel, wall to footing. A chain — and hurricanes are professional weak-link finders. The weak link is almost never a broken beam; it's a connection someone under-nailed. PRO: 'trace the uplift load path' — engineered trusses anchored with hurricane straps embedded in or bolted to the ring beam at EVERY truss; strap-to-truss nailing with EVERY hole filled ('three nails in a ten-hole strap' is the classic shortcut); ring-shank nails; hips outperform gables (no flat end wall catching pressure — relevant at plan selection).

sections.heading: Corners, zones, and the secondary barrier
sections.body: PLAIN: Wind doesn't pull evenly — it pulls hardest at roof corners and edges, two to three times harder than the middle, which is why the nailing pattern TIGHTENS there. And accept now: in a design storm the roof covering WILL lose pieces — the sealed underlayment beneath it decides whether the interior floods. PRO: components-and-cladding zone maps; sheathing nailing 6/6 or 6/4 in edge zones vs 6/12 field; peel-and-stick or sealed underlayment as the secondary water barrier; metal standing-seam preferred over shingles for wind rating and insurer pricing ($9–16/sf vs $4.5–7.5, repaid through premiums and storm performance).

sections.heading: Openings are structure
sections.body: PLAIN: One broken window in a storm lets the wind INSIDE, where it pushes up on the roof from below while the outside sucks up — the two can nearly double the total uplift. That's why impact glass and shutters are structural equipment, not fancy options. PRO: 'internal pressurization' — one breached opening converts the building to partially-enclosed design pressures; opening protection is part of the wind design, and the inspection hold points are strap embedment BEFORE the ring beam pour (retrofit = epoxy anchors at 10x), strap nailing, sheathing pattern by zone, and underlayment laps/penetrations.

quiz.teach: Uplift travels the load path link by link — order is the anatomy.
quiz.prompt: Trace the wind-uplift load path from the storm to the ground:
items: Roof covering resists suction and stays attached
Sheathing, nailed to zone pattern, holds the covering's load
Hurricane straps tie every truss to the ring beam
Ring beam distributes into the wall reinforcement
Wall steel carries down to the footing
Footing bears the fight into the rock
quiz.explanation: PLAIN: every piece hands its pull to the next — a chain from shingle to bedrock. PRO: 'covering → sheathing → truss → strap → bond beam → wall steel → footing.' Hurricanes fail the weakest LINK, and the link is almost always a connection — which is why the inspection program lives at the connections. (S6)

quiz.teach: Uplift pressure is not uniform across a roof.
quiz.prompt: Why does the sheathing nailing pattern tighten at roof edges and corners?

choices.text: Corner and edge uplift runs 2–3x the field pressure — corners are where roofs unzip, so the code's zone maps concentrate fasteners exactly there
choices.why: Correct. Wind accelerating around edges creates the strongest suction at corners; the first panel lost there peels its neighbors — 'unzipping.'

choices.text: Edges are where sheets meet, so more nails close the gaps
choices.why: Joint coverage is a side effect. The driver is aerodynamic: measured corner pressures are multiples of mid-roof.

choices.text: It's conservatism — uniform nailing would do
choices.why: Zone maps come from wind-tunnel and storm-damage data, not caution. Uniform nailing sized for corners wastes field nails; sized for field, loses corners.
Truss stiffness is a different topic — the zones map PRESSURE, not deflection.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: wind pulls hardest at the roof's corners — so that's where the extra nails go. PRO: '6/6 or 6/4 edge-zone nailing vs 6/12 field, ring-shank, verified by zone at inspection.' The pattern IS the wind rating. (S6)

quiz.teach: A building's wind design assumes it stays closed.
quiz.prompt: Why is one breached window a structural event rather than a water problem?

choices.text: The breach pressurizes the interior — inside pushing up while outside sucks up can nearly double net roof uplift, which is why opening protection is part of the structure, not an accessory
choices.why: Correct. 'Internal pressurization': the building becomes a bag being inflated inside a vacuum. Shutters and impact glazing are load-path equipment.

choices.text: Water damage through the opening ruins finishes
choices.why: True and secondary — the structural event is the pressure change, which threatens the ROOF, not the carpet.
A real hazard, but the design-level answer is pressure: one opening changes the load case for the whole roof.

choices.text: It isn't structural if the roof straps are good
choices.why: Straps sized for enclosed-building uplift meet nearly double the load when the envelope breaches — the margin you paid for is spent by one window.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: a storm that gets inside blows the lid off from within — keep it out and the roof only fights half the battle. PRO: 'one breach converts the design to partially-enclosed pressures; opening protection is structural.' (S6, V3-2)

quiz.teach: Suppliers substitute; engineers of record approve.
quiz.prompt: The truss supplier substitutes a strap clip with a lower uplift rating, 'equivalent per their engineer.' What's the acceptance path?

choices.text: YOUR engineer of record reviews and approves — or rejects — the substitution; the supplier's engineer certifies their product, not your building's load path
choices.why: Correct. 'Equivalent' is a claim about their component; whether it serves YOUR design's uplift schedule at YOUR spacing is the EOR's call, in writing, through the submittal process.
Their stamp covers their product's capacity, not its adequacy in your specific load path. Two different professional opinions with two different scopes.
Substitutions through proper review are normal procurement — supply chains change. The principle is REVIEW, not refusal.

choices.text: Accept if the rating difference is under 10%
choices.why: Percentage rules of thumb aren't engineering — margins vary by connection and location. The EOR knows which straps had spare capacity; you don't.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the person who designed your building says yes or no to swapped parts — not the person selling the swap. PRO: 'substitution through the submittal register, EOR approval before purchase' — Module 10's submittal discipline meeting S6's load path. (S6, M10)

mathProblems.title: Metal vs shingle across the program
mathProblems.context: The roofing premium per house times the program: treat houses as both cut and fill, and the per-house delta as the rate — the up-front cost of the better wind rating, to weigh against insurance premiums and storm performance for 302 buyers.

mathProblems.title: The strap retrofit multiplier
mathProblems.context: Straps embedded before the ring-beam pour cost their catalog price. Straps remembered after = epoxy anchors at roughly 10x. Price the forgetting.

decisionPoints.title: Storm at 60% roof completion
decisionPoints.scenario: A tropical storm watch goes up with a house wave at 60% roofs: some houses dried in, some with bare trusses, several with sheathing partially nailed and bundles staged on top. The preparedness plan's 48-hour actions are due. The roofing sub proposes 'nail everything as far as we get and tarp the rest' — maximum progress before landfall.

options.label: Triage per the plan: COMPLETE nailing on nearly-done roofs (a fully-nailed deck is wind-strong), STRIP loose sheathing from barely-started ones (partial decks are sails), ground and band all staged bundles, and photograph everything for insurance
options.outcome: The counterintuitive half — REMOVING material from barely-sheathed roofs — is what the plan exists to have decided in advance: a 30% nailed deck is a wing with pre-started fasteners. The photo record settles the insurance conversation months before it starts.

options.label: Race to nail as much as possible everywhere
options.outcome: The nearly-done roofs benefit; the barely-started ones end up 50% nailed — the worst possible state, enough sheathing to catch wind, not enough nails to hold it. The storm redistributes those panels across the phase, and some into the neighbors' yards.

options.label: Tarp everything and evacuate early
options.outcome: Tarps in tropical-storm wind are confetti with grommets. Early evacuation is right for PEOPLE; for the structures, tarping instead of triage leaves every partial deck exactly as dangerous as the wind finds it.

decisionPoints.debrief: Partial roofs are the most wind-vulnerable state a house passes through, and the correct actions differ BY COMPLETION STATE — finish the finishable, strip the un-holdable, secure the loose, document everything. That triage logic is what a preparedness plan pre-decides, because nobody reasons well at 48 hours. (S6, M1)
